name: PT Darya-Varia Laboratoria Tbk

frontmatter.title: Darya-Varia: the margin problem is prescription, not the brands
frontmatter.summary: Revenue grew at a double-digit pace and profit fell. The segment note shows why: consumer-health gross margin held while prescription gave back a fifth of its margin. Add a fourth quarter that carries the marketing load, one distributor taking most of revenue, and a cost of equity at peer level, and the equity is worth less than the price. SELL after the liquidity haircut.
thesis: The 2026 record revenue is not operating leverage: nine-month revenue reached 1,848 IDR bn while net profit fell to 143 IDR bn [S6].

The margin decline is not a consumer-health discount war: consumer health earned 585 IDR bn of gross profit on 1,049 IDR bn of revenue, a margin flat to up, while prescription gross profit fell to 249 IDR bn on higher revenue [S6].
One distributor, PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari, took 71.0% of revenue in the nine months, and the filing does not disclose the agreement term or pricing [S6].
The balance sheet is a fortress with net cash, but a 7.8% free float must reach 15.0% by the exchange deadline, so a placement is scheduled, not hypothetical [S11].
Fundamental value is Rp1,342 at the target date against a price of Rp1,570; after the house liquidity adjustment the target is Rp940, a negative total return.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether prescription margin stabilises and Q4 carries the usual marketing load
Annual general meeting and final dividend declaration for FY2026
Nine-month 2027 LK: first read on prescription margin and on placement progress toward the float rule

blocks.text: **SELL, twelve-month target Rp940, total return -35.4% against a price of Rp1,570.** What changed in this revision is the analysis and four inputs. The margin story was misattributed: the segment note shows consumer health holding its gross margin while prescription lost about a fifth of its margin, so we rebuilt the gross-margin path by segment, put the fourth quarter's real marketing load into the cost ratio, restored the recurring part of other income, and moved the cost of equity from an out-of-band figure to a peer-consistent 12.0%. Fundamental value is Rp1,342 at the target date, about a seventh below the price before the house liquidity haircut of 30.0% takes the target to Rp940.

The stock trades on 15.5x our FY2026E earnings, 1.2x book and a dividend yield of 4.8% [S0]. For a business earning a high-single-digit return on equity, that is not cheap. The variant view is narrower than the market's and different from our own first draft: DVLA has not lost pricing power in the brands that make most of its revenue. It has lost margin in the institutional prescription business, where the buyer sets the price, and it has a cost base whose fourth quarter is much heavier than the first nine months. Neither is visible in the headline growth.

The prescription reset is the number that matters. In the nine months to September, consumer health earned 585 IDR bn of gross profit on 1,049 IDR bn of revenue; a year earlier it earned 493 IDR bn on a smaller base, so the margin was flat to up [S6]. Prescription earned 249 IDR bn on 593 IDR bn of revenue against 274 IDR bn on 516 IDR bn — revenue growing, gross profit falling [S6]. Export and toll manufacturing, about a tenth of the business, gave back part of a very high prior-year margin [S6]. That is where the group's 54.3% became the 49.9% the nine months are earning.

We do not extrapolate that reset for a decade, and we do not assume it reverses in full. The base case recovers about half of it by FY2030E: prescription margin rising from the earned level toward the mid-forties, consumer health held where it is, export flat. The filing discloses no contract, tender or formulary schedule that fixes prescription pricing, so the sensitivity table is the honest statement of how much the path matters.

Three things move the value, in this order. First, the cost of equity: the first draft used an industry-default beta and a discount rate below the house band; at a peer-consistent 12.0% the DCF is Rp1,143 [S0]. Second, the prescription margin path. Third, the exit: a holder of size cannot sell this position at the screen price, and the exchange's float rule makes that a dated issue rather than a permanent one.

Against that, the balance sheet is genuinely strong: cash of IDR341.6bn against debt of IDR0.2bn, no borrowing, and a dividend paid twice a year without interruption [S7]. A holder who never needs to sell owns a business with a real brand franchise, net cash and a yield near 4.8%. The problem is the price paid for it and the exit, which is what a twelve-month target measures.

Darya-Varia Laboratoria is an Indonesian pharmaceutical manufacturer and marketer listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 1994, controlled by Blue Sphere Singapore Pte Ltd with a 92.1% stake at the end of 2025 [S8]. It runs two c-GMP plants — Gunung Putri for soft-gelatin capsules, liquids, plasters and creams, and Citeureup for sterile injectables and solid dosage — both certified to BPOM standards and to the international quality, environmental and occupational-safety certification families [S8]. It employs 1,344 people [S0].

The company reports three product businesses plus a services line. In FY2025, consumer-health products sold to third parties brought in 1,428 IDR bn, prescription drugs 787 IDR bn, and a further 118 IDR bn and 96.9 IDR bn respectively came from related parties [S7]. Net revenue after 285 IDR bn of sales discounts was IDR2,231.7bn [S7]. More than half the business is consumer health — the brands a reader will recognise: Natur-E in skin nutrition, Enervon-C and Enervon Active in multivitamins, Decolgen and Neozep in cough and cold, Biogesic in analgesics, Diatabs in anti-diarrhoeals [S0]. The next third is prescription, sold through a professional healthcare group to specialists and hospitals across cardiology, gastro-hepatology, antibiotics and women's health [S8].

Distribution is the structure to understand before the P&L. One customer, PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari, is the group's national distributor for both prescription drugs and consumer health products and accounted for 1,306 IDR bn of revenue, net of discounts, in the nine months to September — 71.0% of the group total [S6]. A related party, Concord Pharmaceuticals Ltd, added 133 IDR bn [S6]. The filing does not disclose the term, exclusivity or pricing mechanics of the Anugerah agreement; we searched the annual report and the interim accounts and found no such disclosure, so the concentration has to be treated as an unquantified contract risk rather than a known one.

The strategic story of 2025 and 2026 is diversification away from the plain-vanilla portfolio. The company licensed Pariet, a proton-pump inhibitor, for the Indonesian market from August 2025; it launched Neostrata skin care and a gallstone therapy; and it has begun entering medical devices as a new line [S8]. Management describes the intent as growing at a high single-digit rate each year, above the industry average, by broadening the portfolio and adding products in adjacent categories [S8]. That is a credible plan and it is visible in the revenue line. It is also a plan that runs through in-licensed and bought-in products, which carry a distributor's margin rather than a manufacturer's — one reason the prescription line's gross margin moved as it did.

Scale matters here. DVLA is not a leader in the way the largest listed Indonesian pharmaceutical group is: it is a mid-sized, brand-led challenger with a strong position in a handful of consumer-health categories and a sub-scale prescription business. It does not disclose market share in the annual report, and we have not been able to source a reliable third-party share estimate; we treat the above-market growth claim as a company target rather than an established fact [S8].

The group structure is simple and the controlling shareholder is offshore. Blue Sphere Singapore took over the founders' combined stake, and the public holds the remainder [S8]. Related-party sales run into affiliate distribution companies — Concord Pharmaceuticals, Unam and PT Medifarma Laboratories appear in the related-party note — and together are about a tenth of net revenue [S6]. The related-party exposure is a governance item to monitor, not a value driver; the concentration in the unrelated national distributor is the larger issue.

Indonesia's pharmaceutical market is large, growing and structurally import-dependent. The company's own annual report cites a projected market value of 10.3 USD bn by 2030, driven by the middle class, wider healthcare access and rising demand for health products [S8]. Official statistics put growth of the chemicals, pharmaceuticals and traditional-medicine industry at 8.1% in the third quarter of 2026, so the underlying market is expanding at a rate close to the company's own guidance [S9].

The cost side is where the group margin moved, but not uniformly. The annual report puts imported raw material at 94.0% of the total and describes this as a structural challenge, especially when the rupiah is sliding [S8]. If imported cost were the whole story, every segment would show it. The segment note says otherwise: consumer health, which uses the same imported actives, held its gross margin, while prescription gave back about a fifth of its margin [S6]. Imported cost explains the direction of pressure; the segment split tells you where it landed, and it landed in the channel where the buyer sets the price.

Regulation cuts both ways. The national health insurance programme expands volume but anchors price: the company explicitly commits to competitive pricing for unbranded products in support of the programme [S8]. BPOM, the drug regulator, was recognised as a WHO Listed Authority in December 2025, which the regulator now presents as a platform for attracting investment and shortening approval pathways [S10]. A stronger regulator is good for compliant, c-GMP manufacturers like DVLA and raises the bar for the informal end of the market. The halal certification regime is a further compliance cost that favours scale players.

That distinction is the competitive analysis. In consumer health, the annual report describes intensifying competition in skin health specifically, with many new local and international brands entering and driving price competition and customer-acquisition spending [S8]. In the event, the brands held: the consumer-health gross margin was flat to up on the year and the segment grew faster than the group [S6]. Brand equity in vitamins, cough-and-cold and analgesics is doing real work, and we will not call a discount war the accounts do not show.

In prescription, the annual report describes sustained pricing pressure in the institutional segment and a preference for cheaper generics, with antibiotics, women's health and aesthetic skin care all below expectations as lower-middle-income purchasing power fell [S8]. The nine-month accounts show what that looks like when it bites: revenue up, gross profit down on higher revenue [S6]. The national health insurance programme expands volume but anchors price, and the company explicitly commits to competitive pricing for unbranded products in support of the programme [S8].

Five-forces view. Buyer power is high and rising, because the institutional channel is concentrated and price-led. Supplier power is high for imported active ingredients, and the rupiah does the suppliers' negotiating. The threat of new entrants is high in consumer health, where digital-native brands can launch without a distribution network — the annual report says exactly this [S8] — and low in prescription manufacturing, where c-GMP capacity and BPOM registration are real barriers. Substitutes are generic equivalents, which is the same point as buyer power. Rivalry is intense in both segments.

DVLA's moat is therefore narrower than its brand list and wider than our first draft allowed. Distribution reach into general trade and modern trade is real, and the consumer-health franchise has genuine brand equity — proven by the fact that it held price through an input-cost shock. What it does not have is pricing power in prescription, where a single distributor and a state insurer stand between it and the patient. We treat the consumer franchise as a narrow, stable moat and the prescription business as a commoditising one [S6]. That mix is why the group gross margin does not return to its FY2025 level in our forecast.

Revenue has compounded from IDR1,917.0bn in FY2022 to IDR2,231.7bn in FY2025, a mid-single-digit pace with a strong 2026 acceleration [S0]. The shape of the P&L is unusual for a manufacturer: gross margin above fifty percent, because the company is a brand owner rather than a contract manufacturer, but an operating margin under ten percent, because selling and marketing consumes most of the gross profit [S7]. In FY2025, selling and marketing expense was the single largest cost after cost of revenue, and administration added a further layer [S7]. That structure means small changes in gross margin flow almost one-for-one into net profit, which is precisely what happened in 2026.

The 2026 nine-month LK is the most important document in this report. Revenue reached 1,848 IDR bn, up at a double-digit rate on the prior year, with prescription to third parties growing fastest [S6]. Cost of revenue rose faster still, and sales discounts rose by more than a third to 269 IDR bn [S6]. Gross profit of 923 IDR bn implies a margin near 49.9%, against the 54.3% earned in FY2025 [S6][S7]. Operating profit fell from 216 IDR bn to 187 IDR bn, and net profit of 143 IDR bn was below the prior-year nine months [S6]. Net operating cash flow fell to 122 IDR bn from 192 IDR bn a year earlier, down by about a third, because inventories rose to 579 IDR bn and receivables grew with the sales [S6].

The segment note is the analysis, and it changes the story. In the nine months, consumer health earned 585 IDR bn of gross profit on 1,049 IDR bn of revenue — a share slightly above the 493 IDR bn earned a year earlier on a smaller base — while prescription earned 249 IDR bn on 593 IDR bn against 274 IDR bn on 516 IDR bn [S6]. Export and toll manufacturing earned 83.4 IDR bn on a similar base, down from a very high prior-year margin [S6]. The whole of the group decline sits in prescription and export; the branded consumer franchise did not lose price. We have found no filing disclosure that fixes the cause or the duration of the prescription reset — no contract, tender or formulary schedule — so we treat it as a pricing and mix event, half of which laps and half of which is structural.

For FY2026E we model revenue of IDR2,521.9bn, growth of 13.0%, which is the reported nine months plus a fourth quarter growing slightly slower than the nine-month pace. We hold gross margin at 49.9% — the level the LK is actually earning, not a recovery — then recover to 51.6% by FY2030E on a segment build: consumer health held at its earned margin, prescription recovering about half of the reset, export flat [S6][S8]. The terminal margin is 51.6%, below the FY2025 level and above the trough.

The cost ratio needed rebuilding, and the fourth quarter is why. FY2025 selling and marketing plus administration was IDR1,006.9bn on IDR2,231.7bn of revenue, and the fourth quarter alone carried a far higher intensity than the first nine months: the year's operating profit of IDR205.9bn was essentially all earned by September, with 216 IDR bn already booked [S7][S6]. The quarter's trading result was negative before net other income; the LK's reported operating profit is struck after it, which is why the quarter looks flat rather than loss-making. The nine months of 2026 ran at a lower ratio than the nine months of 2025, so there is modest operating leverage in the first three quarters, but a fourth quarter at the intensity FY2025 actually carried gives a full-year ratio close to the prior year, not the lower number a straight-line nine-month run rate implies. We set FY2026E at 44.4% and hold it near that level, allowing only the nine-month improvement to persist [S6][S7]. On those inputs FY2026E net profit is IDR113.6bn and EPS Rp101 [S0].

The out-years grow revenue at a decelerating pace, from high single digits to mid single digits, in line with the company's stated ambition and the industry's current growth rate, and hold the cost ratios where the last actual put them [S8][S9]. That produces net profit of IDR197.3bn in FY2030E and a return on equity rising from 11.2% to 11.4%, mechanically, because a payout of about three-quarters means equity compounds slowly while earnings grow [S0].

Other income is a real, recurring line and we no longer zero it. The other-income note shows shared-service fees from a related party of 3.2 IDR bn in the nine months, laboratory and validation services, and bank charges recurring every period; fixed-asset sale gains and foreign-exchange moves are not [S6]. We capitalise IDR8.0bn a year, below the net other income reported in FY2024 and FY2025, and leave the asset-sale gains out [S7]. Zeroing it, as the first draft did, was a default haircut the house method does not allow.

The D&A line needed restating and we restated it. The data pack carries a depreciation charge of a fraction of the real one, a known artefact of the Indonesian direct-method cash-flow presentation. The notes to the FY2025 accounts show depreciation of 68.0 IDR bn for FY2025 and 60.3 IDR bn for FY2024, allocated across cost of revenue, selling and administration [S7]. We put both into the model as facts, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR273.9bn and the margin to 12.3% [S0][S7]. That EBITDA is operating profit before other income plus D&A; the LK's operating profit of IDR205.9bn is struck after net other income of IDR9.4bn, so the LK's operating-profit-plus-D&A figure is about that much higher than our EBITDA line. We keep other income as its own input rather than inside EBITDA, and use the same definition throughout. The charge is a real economic cost and the cash-flow statement shows the capex that goes with it: IDR107.3bn in FY2025, about 4.8% of sales, which we hold flat [S7].

Working capital is the quiet drag on this business. Operating working capital was IDR643.2bn at the end of FY2025, 28.8% of revenue, and receivables run at more than four months of sales [S7]. At any growth rate, that structure consumes cash: our model shows a working-capital build of IDR83.1bn in FY2026E alone, which is why free cash flow to the firm is only IDR-23.2bn on IDR113.6bn of net profit [S0]. The company collects slowly because its customer is a distributor with more bargaining power than the manufacturer, and it holds high inventory because imported active ingredients have long lead times. Neither is mismanagement; both are permanent features of the cash cycle and both are in the valuation.

Balance-sheet health is excellent and there is nothing hidden in it. Cash was IDR341.6bn at the FY2025 year end and IDR256.3bn on our forecast, with debt limited to lease liabilities [S6][S7]. Total equity was IDR1,479.8bn, book value per share Rp1,321 [S0]. There is no refinancing risk, no covenant, and no need for the capital markets. Capital allocation is conservative: maintenance and capacity capex at roughly a twentieth of sales, a twice-yearly dividend of about three-quarters of earnings, and no acquisitions since the 2014 merger [S7][S8].

Earnings quality, run against the house screens. Cash conversion is not a problem: operating cash flow was 201 IDR bn in FY2025 and 332 IDR bn in FY2024 against net profit of IDR163.9bn and IDR156.1bn — above one in both years and above one cumulatively, so the three-year accruals picture is negative accruals, not earnings outrunning cash [S7]. The nine-month gap runs the other way: 122 IDR bn of operating cash flow on 143 IDR bn of net profit, which is the inventory and receivables build, not a change in accounting [S6]. Receivables are growing broadly with revenue — the distributor balance is stable — while inventory is growing faster than cost of revenue, which we flag but do not treat as manipulation: imported-ingredient stocking explains it [S6]. The IDX regime flags are clean on the registry snapshot of 27 October 2026: DVLA is not on the high-shareholding-concentration list, has had no index deletion and no enforcement action; its issue is the opposite — a free float of 7.8% against the exchange's 15.0% minimum, which is a supply event rather than a governance one [S11]. The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion from a Big Four auditor [S7][S8]. Related-party sales are about a tenth of revenue and disclosed [S6]. Our conclusion is that the earnings are real and the problem is margins, not accounting.

We value DVLA primarily on discounted free cash flow to the firm, which is the right method for a branded pharmaceutical manufacturer with predictable volume, no commodity price exposure and a long operating history. There is no sum-of-the-parts here — the two segments share manufacturing, distribution and overheads — and no asset value worth anchoring to, since the plants are worth more as a going concern than in liquidation. The multiple cross-checks are there to test the DCF, not to set the target.

The discount rate now ties to its own build and sits inside the house band. The engine's cost of equity before any company adjustment is 7.4% risk-free, less a 1.6% default spread, plus a beta of 0.70 times the sum of the 4.2% mature-market premium and the 2.5% Indonesia country premium; 12.0% is that figure plus the 1.5% company premium. Two disclosures the first draft owed the reader: the beta is the industry default, not a DVLA regression (the house beta file has no PHARMA median), and the default-spread term is negative — it reduces the rate rather than adding to it. We therefore add an explicit company premium for the two risks a sector beta does not price: a single distributor taking most of revenue and a free float the exchange requires to treble. That puts the cost of equity at 12.0%, at the level of the peer set (KLBF, SIDO and TSPC all above twelve percent on the same engine), and the WACC equals it at 12.0% because the company carries no net debt [S0]. The first draft's figure was below the house band and is withdrawn.

The DCF produces Rp1,143 per share, with 58.8% of the value in the terminal period [S0]. The explicit forecast contributes the rest: five years of free cash flow that average well below net profit because working capital absorbs the growth, and a terminal value that assumes 4.5% nominal growth forever, which is roughly Indonesian CPI plus a point of real growth and is below nominal GDP [S0][S8]. We checked the terminal assumption against the reinvestment it implies: the model reinvests about two-fifths of NOPAT to grow at that rate, which is consistent with earning no more than the cost of capital in perpetuity. There is no value creation after the forecast horizon in this valuation, and no multiple expansion: the implied exit EV/EBITDA is below the multiple the stock trades on today.

The cross-checks are both on trailing metrics, and the report should say so plainly. The PE method applies a peer-median 10.5 to the pack's last-twelve-month earnings, giving Rp1,336; the EV/EBITDA method applies 7.0 to last-twelve-month EBITDA, giving Rp1,604 [S0]. Neither uses the FY2026E figures: on our forward EBITDA the same multiple would give a materially higher number, which is why the EV/EBITDA cross-check now sits well above the DCF and is flagged. That gap is not a reason to prefer it. Trailing EBITDA is a trough that still contains the pre-reset prescription margin and none of the recovery; capitalising it at a peer multiple would double-count the trough. We keep both cross-checks because they bracket the DCF from below and above, apply the fixed weights of sixty, thirty and ten percent, and do not use the blend to lift the target. The weighted value is Rp1,342 at the target date.

Then the liquidity adjustment, which is the single largest number in this report and the reason the rating is SELL rather than HOLD. DVLA's three-month average daily traded value is 55,677,968.3 rupiah, orders of magnitude below the fund's threshold, and the free float is 7.8% [S0]. The house rule applies an explicit 30.0% haircut to the target, shown as its own line rather than buried in the discount rate, and that takes Rp1,342 to Rp940. On fundamental value alone the total return would be a high single-digit negative — enough for HOLD, not enough for a positive call. The haircut is what makes it a SELL, and we say so rather than dress it up as a fundamental view.

What the price implies. At Rp1,570 the stock trades on 15.5x FY2026E earnings, 1.2x book and a dividend yield of 4.8% on our forecast [S0]. To justify that price on our assumptions you need a lower discount rate than 12.0% or terminal growth above 4.5%; the market is, in effect, treating the prescription margin reset as temporary and paying a consumer-health multiple for a business that is now part brands and part institutional. Our base case says the brands deserve the multiple and the prescription arm does not.

The float rule changes the exit, not the value, and it cuts both ways. The free float is 7.8% against a 15.0% minimum; to reach it on a share count of IDR1,120.0bn million, the controlling shareholder has to release roughly eighty million shares by the exchange's deadline in 2029 [S11]. That is scheduled supply, and over time it should compress the liquidity discount. It is also why the current haircut is defensible today: nothing about the next twelve months changes the traded value. A holder who can wait past the placement owns a more liquid stock; a holder measuring a twelve-month return does not.
The risks that matter, in order of what they would do to the value.

**Customer concentration — high likelihood, high impact.** One distributor, PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari, took 71.0% of revenue in the nine months and a related party 133 IDR bn; the agreement's term and pricing mechanics are not disclosed [S6]. If terms are reset, or the relationship changes hands, most of the revenue is renegotiated at once. This is the largest single-company risk in the file and it sits behind the cost-of-equity premium.

**Prescription margin — reset confirmed, duration unknown — high likelihood, high impact.** Prescription gross profit fell on higher revenue and its margin by a fifth [S6]. The filing does not say whether the cause is tender pricing, mix toward in-licensed goods, or a one-off rebate, so the recovery cannot be dated. Our base case recovers half; the bear case assumes none and some spillover into consumer health.

**Currency and input costs — high likelihood, medium impact.** With almost all raw material imported, further rupiah depreciation passes into cost of revenue with a lag [S8]. Our macro deck already has the rupiah weaker in FY2027E than today, so the base case carries some of this [S0]. The segment evidence says a weak rupiah is not sufficient on its own to break the consumer franchise, which held margin through the 2026 move.

**Competitive intensity in consumer health — medium likelihood, medium impact.** New digital-native brands in skin health and supplements are raising customer-acquisition costs, which shows up as sales discounts [S6][S8]. The brands have so far held price; the bear case is that they stop.

**Execution on the diversification — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Medical devices and licensed products such as Pariet are new competences for a branded manufacturer [S8]. They also carry lower gross margins than own-manufactured brands, so success can dilute margin even as it grows revenue.

**Governance and control — low likelihood, high impact.** A 92.1% controlling shareholder with a 7.8% float means minority holders have no practical influence, related-party sales run through an affiliate distributor, and a placement is coming [S6][S11]. We found no evidence of value leakage and the auditor is unimpaired, but the structure concentrates risk [S8].
**Liquidity — certain, high impact on a twelve-month horizon.** Daily turnover of 55,677,968.3 rupiah is the binding constraint on the rating, not the fundamentals [S0].

The scenarios are mirrored: the bear cuts four points off revenue growth and a point and a half off gross margin, the bull adds the same amounts, and the probabilities are a quarter, a half and a quarter [S0]. On target-date values the bear case is Rp1,176, the base Rp1,321 and the bull Rp1,551; today's values, before the roll-forward and the dividend deduction, are lower at Rp1,099, Rp1,247 and Rp1,472 respectively. The range is narrow for an equity: this is not a business whose value swings with a commodity price. The asymmetry in the rating comes from the liquidity haircut, which applies in every scenario, not from the operating outcomes.

What would change our mind, in either direction: two consecutive quarters of stable prescription gross margin, with consumer health still holding, would say the reset has bottomed and move us toward the bull case. A widening of the discount line relative to gross sales would say the opposite. A placement that lifted the float, or a buyback at a discount to book, would change the liquidity adjustment and therefore the rating without changing the fundamentals at all — and on our numbers it is the placement, not the P&L, that a twelve-month holder should watch.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Blue Sphere Singapore Pte Ltd holds 92.1% of the shares, having taken over the founders' combined stake; the public holds the rest, and institutions are effectively absent at 1.2% [S8][S0]. There is no evidence of a pledged controlling stake in the filings we reviewed, and the company's receivables are explicitly unpledged [S8]. The board is led by a president director and a finance director, with a separate internal audit unit and corporate secretary function [S0].

The free float is the governance fact that matters most this year. At 7.8% against the exchange's 15.0% minimum, DVLA is below the threshold, and its market capitalisation puts it in the tier with the longest transition deadline [S11]. That implies a placement of roughly eighty million shares by 2029, which dilutes the controlling stake rather than the earnings and which the company has not yet announced. We treat it as scheduled supply and a positive for liquidity, not as a governance failure.

The auditor is KAP Purwantono, Sungkoro & Surja (Ernst & Young), which audited the FY2025 accounts and provided no non-audit services in the period [S8]. The opinion is unqualified in the FY2025 financial statements [S7]. That combination — Big Four, no non-audit work, clean opinion — is the governance baseline we want and it is met.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and material enough to watch. Sales to affiliates are about a tenth of net revenue, with Concord Pharmaceuticals the largest at 133 IDR bn in the nine months; purchases from a related toll manufacturer and royalties to a related licensor are also disclosed [S6]. The royalty line is the one to monitor: it is charged against selling and marketing and grows with the licensed-product portfolio, so a shift toward in-licensed products raises a related-party cost at the same time as it lowers gross margin. We do not see this as a value-destruction channel at current scale, but it is the item to re-check every year.

The dividend record is the strongest part of the governance story: an interim and a final payment every year, about three-quarters of earnings, paid through the cycle without a cut [S7]. For a controlling shareholder that could retain cash, this is a meaningful choice in favour of minorities. Our forecast keeps the payout at 74.0%.

ESG exposures are ordinary for the sector. The company operates c-GMP plants with environmental management certification, reports under GRI, and is exposed to the halal-certification regime and to BPOM inspection standards [S8][S10]. The material ESG risk is the same as the commercial one: an import-dependent supply chain that is exposed to currency and to global active-ingredient availability. Product quality and pharmacovigilance are the tail risks that matter in this industry, and a WHO-listed regulator is a mitigant rather than a guarantee [S10].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in March 2027, the annual general meeting and final dividend in June, and the nine-month 2027 LK in October. The March results matter most: they will show whether prescription gross margin has stabilised and whether the fourth quarter repeats its usual marketing load, which the first nine months cannot tell you [S6].

Between updates we monitor five things. Prescription gross margin, quarterly, from the segment note: this is the thesis. Consumer-health gross margin: if it starts to give back the ground it held while prescription fell, the discount war we did not find in 2026 has arrived. The ratio of sales discounts to gross sales: if it keeps rising faster than gross sales, pricing is being bought [S6]. Inventory and receivables days: working capital is already absorbing most of the free cash flow, and a further deterioration would cut the dividend cover [S7]. And the free float and traded value: a placement that lifts the float above the house threshold would remove the haircut and, all else equal, move the target toward fundamental value [S11].
We also watch the rupiah. The macro deck has it at Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E, and every further step weaker is a cost event for the prescription business in particular [S0].

S11.title: BEI Umumkan 327 Emiten Belum Penuhi Ketentuan Free Float 15 Persen : Okezone Economy

valuation.label: P/E
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

valuation.label: EV/EBITDA
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The prescription reset is permanent and spreads: tender and JKN formulary pricing keeps prescription margin at the 42% earned in 2026, the discount step does not lap, and consumer health finally gives back part of its 55.7% as digital-native brands buy shelf space. Growth slows to 9%.

bull.narrative: The prescription reset proves to be pricing and mix, not structure: the 2026 discount step laps, licensed products settle into the portfolio, and prescription margin recovers faster while consumer health holds 55.7%. Revenue keeps the 9M-26 pace and the rupiah steadies.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 13.0% is the arithmetic of the reported nine months (revenue +13.5% to Rp1,848.5bn, LK Sep-2026 p.7) plus a Q4 at +11.5% yoy, deliberately below the 9M run-rate because Q4-2025 carried the year-end marketing push. FY2027E-30E step down to 8.0/7.5/7.0/6.5%: the company guides 7-9% for 2026 and aims to grow above the industry (AR2025 p.73), while the chem/pharma industry grew 8.1% in Q3-2026. No volume haircut: units grew through 9M-26.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from note 28 segment gross margins, not from a group discount-war story. 9M-2026 [S6 p.82]: consumer health 55.74% (584.957/1,049.409) against 55.31% a year earlier - flat to up; prescription 42.07% (249.419/592.827) against 53.13%, down 11.1pp; export and toll manufacturing 41.47% against 47.81%; group 49.93% against 54.41%. The whole 4.5pp group decline sits in prescription and export; the branded consumer franchise (57% of revenue) did not lose price. FY2026E is the earned 49.9% with Q4 held at that level. Thereafter group GM rises to 51.6% by FY2030E on the note 28 weights: consumer held at 56%, prescription recovering 4.5pp of the 11.1pp reset to 46.5% as the 2026 discount step laps and licensed-product mix settles, export held at 41.5%. That is a half-recovery, well short of FY2025's 53.0% prescription margin. No FX tailwind: the macro deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 in FY2027E vs 17,968 spot [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Quarterly bridge, not a round number. 9M-2026 selling and marketing plus administration was Rp750.1bn, 40.6% of revenue, against 41.5% in 9M-2025 [S6 p.7]. FY2025 Q4 carried Rp330.8bn of SG&A on Rp603.6bn of revenue = 54.8% [S7 p.16], the year-end marketing and accrual load. FY2026E is 9M actual plus a Q4 at that same 54.8% intensity on our Q4 revenue: 44.4% of the year. We then hold ~44% flat, allowing only the 0.4pp of nine-month operating leverage already visible to carry into later years. We do not assume the Q4 load shrinks. Full-year FY2025 was 45.07% (Rp1,005.9bn on Rp2,231.7bn) [S7 p.16].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation expense was Rp68.0bn in FY2025 and Rp60.3bn in FY2024 (note 9), not the data pack's Rp41.3bn. That is 3.05% of FY2025 revenue and is held flat; the separately disclosed investment-property depreciation (Rp2.6bn) sits in administration and is not added, so the charge is, if anything, slightly understated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was Rp107.3bn in FY2025 (4.81% of revenue) and Rp74.0bn in 9M-2026 (4.01%), funding the two c-GMP plants at Gunung Putri and Citeureup plus the medical-device diversification; both are shown in the cash-flow statements. Held at the last actual 4.8% with no capacity step-up, since no new plant has been announced.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 28.8% is the FY2025 actual (current assets less cash, less current liabilities: Rp1,664.5bn - Rp341.6bn - Rp679.9bn = Rp643.2bn on Rp2,231.7bn revenue). 9M-2026 shows the same intensity: inventory Rp578.6bn and receivables Rp899.4bn against revenue of Rp1,848.5bn, with trade payables up to Rp265.9bn. No release is assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate was 25.5% (tax Rp56.2bn on pre-tax Rp220.2bn) and 24.8% for 9M-2026; the statutory 22% plus non-deductible items. Held at 25.0%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Essentially debt-free: finance costs were Rp32m in FY2025 and Rp4.5m in 9M-2026 on lease liabilities only. Cost of debt set at 9.0%, the overdraft rate, and irrelevant to value.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income Rp4.99bn on opening cash of Rp357.8bn = 1.40%; 9M-2026 finance income Rp2.93bn on Rp341.6bn. Set at 1.4%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing planned; the company is in net cash (Rp324.3bn cash against Rp0.1bn of lease debt at 30 Sep 2026) and funds capex and dividends from operations.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Recurring portion of net other income, not zero. Note 24 [S6 p.71] for 9M-2026: shared-service fees from PT Medifarma Rp3.23bn (related party, recurring), laboratory and validation services Rp1.10bn, bank charges Rp0.32bn and other charges Rp0.32bn; fixed-asset sale gains Rp3.91bn and net FX gains Rp1.46bn are excluded as non-recurring. That is Rp5.8bn for nine months = Rp7.7bn annualised; we set Rp8.0bn flat, which also leaves a small margin for the 'other' line (Rp5.5bn in 9M) without capitalising asset-sale gains. Net other income was +Rp9.0bn FY2024 and +Rp9.4bn FY2025 [S7 p.16], so this is below the last two actuals, not above.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interest is Rp1.1m on the balance sheet; under 0.01% of profit. Zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Cash dividends of Rp120.96bn were paid in FY2025 on net profit of Rp163.9bn = 73.8% (statement of cash flows p.19; equity statement p.18), and Rp71.68bn again in 9M-2026. DVLA pays an interim and a final every year. 74% held; no step-up assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 1,120,000,000 shares issued and paid up, unchanged since the 2014 merger; no rights issue or buyback announced.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.5%: the macro deck's long-run Indonesian CPI of 3.28% plus ~1.2% real, below the 5.0% IDR cap and below nominal GDP (real 5.29% + CPI). It is the growth of a mature domestic pharma distributor, not of the 8-9% current market.

challenges.challenge: The report's causal thesis — consumer-health discount wars are eroding the franchise, and 'the habit is being paid for with discounts' — is contradicted by note 28 of the very LK it cites. Segment gross margins, 9M-2026 vs 9M-2025 [S6 p.82]: consumer health 55.74% (584.957/1,049.409) against 55.31% (493.455/892.088), i.e. flat to up; prescription 42.07% (249.419/592.827) against 53.13% (274.398/516.491), down 11.1pp; export and toll manufacturing 41.47% against 47.81%, down 6.3pp. Group 49.93% against 54.41%. The entire 4.5pp group decline sits in prescription and export, and the AR itself attributes it to imported API raising prescription cost of revenue and institutional buyers preferring cheaper generics [S8 p.57]. The report also says 'prescription to third parties growing fastest' [S6]: third-party consumer revenue rose 17.6% (1,049.4 vs 892.1) and third-party prescription 14.8% (592.8 vs 516.5), so consumer grew faster. The 50.0% flat-GM base case, the consumer-health bear/bull shocks and the quarterly gross-margin monitoring are all built on the wrong segment.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the gross-margin path by segment from note 28: consumer health 55.74% vs 55.31%, prescription 42.07% vs 53.13%, export 41.47% vs 47.81%, group 49.93% vs 54.41%. The report now says the decline is prescription and export, not a consumer discount war; base case recovers half the prescription reset to about 46.5% by FY2030.

challenges.challenge: The opex assumption is justified by a figure the cited filing does not contain. §3 and §7 state FY2025 Q4 operating profit was -Rp4.2bn and 'turned negative on year-end marketing'. FY2025 operating profit is Rp216.226bn [S7 p.16] and 9M-2025 is Rp215.859bn [S6 p.7], so Q4-2025 operating profit was +Rp0.367bn. Q4 gross profit less selling, marketing and administration is -Rp3.98bn only before Rp4.35bn of net other income. The negative figure appears twice and carries the 42.5% opex ratio, which is itself below the last actual (see C3).
challenges.answer: Corrected: FY2025 Q4 operating profit was +Rp0.37bn (FY2025 Rp216.2bn less 9M-2025 Rp215.9bn), negative only before Rp4.35bn of net other income. Section 3 and the catalysts no longer claim a negative quarter; the opex bridge is re-derived on the Q4 intensity actually incurred.

challenges.challenge: The base case is described as conservative on costs but is 2.6pp optimistic. FY2025 selling and marketing (Rp757.5bn) plus administration (Rp248.4bn) was Rp1,005.9bn, 45.07% of revenue [S7 p.16]; FY2026E is set at 42.5%, which requires Q4-2026 opex of Rp321.7bn on Rp673.4bn of revenue (47.8%) against the 54.8% Q4-2025 actually incurred (Rp331.8bn on Rp603.6bn). Even allowing for the 0.9pp improvement in the 9M ratio, a repeated Q4 intensity gives about 43.9%. Each 1pp of opex ratio is worth roughly 20% of the DCF (~Rp340/share), so 1.4-2.6pp is Rp470-880/share that the base case quietly banks and the bear case never tests.
challenges.answer: Opex ratio rebuilt quarter by quarter: 9M-2026 SG&A Rp750.1bn (40.6%) plus a Q4 at the 54.8% intensity FY2025 actually carried (Rp330.8bn on Rp603.6bn) gives 44.4% for FY2026E, held near that level. FY2025 was 45.07% on Rp1,005.9bn; the first draft's 42.5% is withdrawn and the sensitivity table shows the effect.

challenges.challenge: Three-quarters of revenue flows through one distributor and the report never says so. Note 20 [S7 p.77] discloses PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari at Rp1,648.1bn, 74% of revenue (75% in FY2024), and Concord Pharmaceuticals Ltd — a related party — at Rp213.8bn, a further 10%. §3 describes the customer base as 'distributors, hospitals and modern-trade chains', which implies diversification that does not exist, and §5's risk list ranks currency and institutional pricing ahead of a single-counterparty dependence that could remove 74% of revenue. It also means the working-capital build is a bargaining-power problem, not just an import lead-time problem.
challenges.answer: Disclosed and ranked first: PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari took 71% of revenue in 9M-2026 (74% in FY2025) and related party Concord a further Rp132.998bn; the AR and LK do not disclose the agreement's term, exclusivity or pricing, which the report now states. It is the first risk and the basis of the company cost-of-equity premium.

challenges.challenge: Net other income is set to zero as 'not capitalised', but it is recurring and growing: +Rp9.0bn in FY2024 (17.888 less 8.860), +Rp9.4bn in FY2025 (21.967 less 12.607) and +Rp14.6bn in 9M-2026 (15.216 less 0.643), composed of shared-service fees Rp3.2bn, fixed-asset sale gains Rp3.9bn, laboratory services Rp1.1bn, FX Rp1.5bn and other Rp5.5bn [S6 note 24]. Zeroing a line that has been positive in every period shown cuts run-rate net profit by Rp7-11bn, 5-7%, and is the kind of default haircut the house base-case card prohibits. The bull case never gets it back.
challenges.answer: Recurring other income is now capitalised at Rp8.0bn a year: shared-service fees Rp3.23bn (9M), laboratory and validation Rp1.10bn, bank and other charges Rp0.64bn; fixed-asset sale gains Rp3.91bn and FX Rp1.46bn excluded. That is below the FY2024 and FY2025 actual net other income, so it is not a haircut.

challenges.challenge: The report says the controlling shareholder's 92.1% stake 'means the float is unlikely to widen' and treats a placement as hypothetical. It is not hypothetical: BEI announcement Peng-S-00011/BEI.PLP/04-2026 (30 Apr 2026) requires issuers with market capitalisation below Rp5tn to reach a 15% free float by 31 March 2029; DVLA is at 7.76% (IDXIC snapshot, 10 Nov 2026) and its Rp1.76tn market cap puts it in that tier, so about 81m shares (7.24% of 1.12bn) must be released within roughly 28 months. Since the 30% haircut is the single largest number in the target and it exists only because ADTV is Rp55.7m, a scheduled float increase is the one catalyst that changes the rating without changing the fundamentals. §5 mentions the mechanism but calls it hypothetical and cites no rule.
challenges.answer: Cited the exchange's 15% minimum free float and quantified the gap: 7.76% held, 7.24pp short, about 81m of 1.12bn shares to be released by 31 Mar 2029 for the sub-Rp5tn tier. The 30% haircut is retained for a 12-month horizon because traded value is unchanged today; the report shows the target without it would be a HOLD, and names the placement as the catalyst.

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin path is the valuation, and it is set at the trough for a decade. GM starts at 49.9%, reaches 51.0% only in FY2030E and is held at 51.0% in perpetuity, while the AR attributes roughly half the 2026 decline to imported API cost inflation that is a lagged, re-priceable cost and the macro deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 for FY2027E against 17,968 spot — about 2% further depreciation, not a continuing slide. Because 63% of the DCF is terminal value, each permanent 1pp of GM is worth about 20% of the DCF (~Rp340/share): a 2.5pp recovery to 52.5% would take the DCF from Rp1,676 to about Rp2,530. The report's 'no FX tailwind is assumed' is defensible; treating a cyclical input-cost squeeze as a permanent margin reset is not, and no source supports the permanence.
challenges.answer: Gross margin is no longer held at the trough for a decade. Segment build: consumer health at its earned 55.7%, prescription recovering 4.5pp of the 11.1pp reset to 46.5% by FY2030, export flat, giving 51.6% terminal. No full mean reversion to FY2025 is assumed because no filing fixes prescription pricing.

challenges.challenge: The discount-rate paragraph does not reproduce its own number. Stated inputs are rf 7.4%, mature ERP 4.2%, Indonesia country premium 2.5% and a levered beta of 0.70, which sum to 12.1% (12.8% with the country premium added outside the beta), not 10.5%. The engine reaches 10.51% only by deducting an undisclosed 1.62% 'default spread' (fund record valuation.coc: rf 0.0745, default_spread 0.0162, beta 0.70) and it uses the PHARMA template default beta, not a DVLA regression. DVLA's COE is the lowest in its own peer set — KLBF 12.04%, SIDO 12.02%, TSPC 12.37%, SOHO 11.02% — and the report justifies this as being 'at the low end of the band ... deliberately so' without mentioning either the deduction or the beta source. At the peer-implied beta (~0.87, COE 11.65%) the DCF falls from Rp1,676 to about Rp1,450, below the Rp1,570 price, which reverses the report's claim that fundamental value sits above the market.
challenges.answer: COE build now ties out: rf 7.45% less 1.62% default spread plus 0.70 x (4.2% + 2.5%) = 10.51%, plus a disclosed 1.45pp company premium for distributor concentration and float, giving 11.96%. The beta source (industry default, no PHARMA regression median) and the negative spread term are stated; the out-of-band 10.51% is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The cross-checks are capitalised on trough trailing metrics and then described as corroboration. The engine's PE method uses LTM np_parent of Rp142.285bn, not the FY2026E Rp145.428bn the report names (Rp1,336 versus Rp1,366), and the EV/EBITDA method uses LTM EBITDA of Rp210.794bn against FY2026E EBITDA of Rp266.058bn — 21% lower. At the stated 6.98x on FY2026E EBITDA the cross-check is about Rp1,948, not Rp1,604, i.e. 16% above the DCF rather than 'close to' it. The report explains the DCF-PE gap as trough earnings but does not apply the same reasoning to EV/EBITDA, and the 60/30/10 blend therefore weights the trough twice while asking the DCF to capitalise a recovery.
challenges.answer: Both cross-checks are now stated as LTM metric times trailing peer multiple: PE 10.5x on LTM earnings Rp142.3bn = Rp1,336; EV/EBITDA 7.0x on LTM EBITDA Rp210.8bn = Rp1,604, which is 40% above the DCF and flagged. Forward EBITDA would be higher and is deliberately not used; the trough is not double-counted and the 60/30/10 weights are unchanged.

challenges.challenge: §5 reports 'the bear case values the equity at Rp1,329, the base at Rp1,567 and the bull at Rp1,922', while the summary and §4 report a fundamental value of Rp1,667 on a base scenario of Rp1,635. Both are model outputs: 1,329/1,567/1,922 are today's values before the 12-month roll-forward and DPS deduction, and 1,394/1,635/2,005 are the target values (fund record scenarios). A reader cannot tie §5 to the stated target and may read the base case as Rp1,567. Separately, the Rp273.9bn FY2025 EBITDA cited in §3 is the model's pre-other-income figure; the LK's operating profit plus D&A is Rp284.3bn (12.7%), so the calibration anchor and the reported 12.3% margin are model constructs, not filing numbers.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now labels the scenario values at the target date (Rp1,176 / Rp1,321 / Rp1,551) and gives today's values separately (Rp1,099 / Rp1,247 / Rp1,472). FY2025 EBITDA is reconciled: the model's Rp273.9bn is operating profit before other income plus restated D&A; adding the Rp9.4bn net other income approximates the LK's operating-profit-plus-D&A figure.

challenges.challenge: Three editing and screen-completeness failures. §1 says the company 'employs IDR1,344.0bn people' — a unit error from a template slot. §3 says operating cash flow 'halved to 122 IDR bn'; it fell 36% from Rp191.8bn, not 50%. And the earnings-quality section gives no accruals ratio, no cash-conversion trend and says the IDX regime flags 'cannot be checked because the exchange's site refuses scripted access', although the house registry (konglo profile, registry asof 2026-10-27) carries HSC status, index deletions and enforcement, and the free-float snapshot is refreshed to 10 Nov 2026.
challenges.answer: Fixed both errors: headcount renders as 1,344 people, not IDR1,344.0bn, and operating cash flow is shown falling to Rp122.3bn from Rp191.8bn, about a third. Earnings quality now carries three-period cash conversion (CFO Rp331.8bn FY2024, Rp201.1bn FY2025, Rp122.3bn 9M-2026) and the registry status: not HSC, no index deletion, no enforcement, float 7.76% vs 15%.

missing_bull_case.note: Three sourced upsides absent: net other income zeroed although it was +Rp9.0bn FY2024, +Rp9.4bn FY2025 and +Rp14.6bn in 9M-2026 (S6 note 24); the BEI rule forcing the free float to 15% by 31 Mar 2029 from 7.76% now (konglo S25), which would retire the 30% haircut; and consumer-health segment gross margin actually stable at 55.7% (S6 note 28), which contradicts the 'franchise impaired' framing.

missing_bear_case.note: Omits the customer concentration that matters most: PT Anugerah Pharmindo Lestari is Rp1,648.1bn, 74% of revenue (75% in FY2024), and related-party Concord Pharmaceuticals a further 10% (S7 p.77). Also absent: the prescription segment's 11.1pp gross-margin collapse, the 2.6pp opex assumption below the last actual, and any bear case in which terminal growth or the multiple falls.

assumption_realism.note: Gross margin is held at the 9M-2026 trough (49.9%) and lifted only 1.0pp by FY2030E with no source for permanence, while note 28 shows the drop is prescription (-11.1pp) and export/toll (-6.3pp), not consumer health. Opex at 42.5% is 2.6pp below the FY2025 actual 45.1% and implies a Q4-2026 ratio of 47.8% against 54.8% actually incurred. Every 1pp of either ratio moves the DCF about 20%.

evidence_and_citations.note: Two load-bearing misstatements: Q4-2025 operating profit is quoted as -Rp4.2bn although the LK gives +Rp0.4bn, and the PE cross-check is described as FY2026E earnings when the engine uses LTM Rp142.3bn. §5's scenario values do not tie to the target, 'employs IDR1,344.0bn people' is a unit error, and 'cash flow halved' is -36%. The core facts (revenue, gross profit, NP, discounts, D&A, 74%/94%/92.12%) all verify.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF as primary is right for the industry and the bridge is right (net cash Rp324.3bn at 30 Sep 2026, minorities nil, no post-balance-sheet items). But the PE and EV/EBITDA cross-checks capitalise trough LTM metrics (EBITDA Rp210.8bn vs FY2026E Rp266.1bn; NP Rp142.3bn vs Rp145.4bn), so the 30% and 10% weights penalise the same trough the DCF is asked to look through, and the EV/EBITDA 'close to the DCF' is 21% higher on forward EBITDA.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the model. Fundamental value is Rp1,667 against a price of Rp1,570 and the pre-haircut 12-month total return is +12.3% (an ADD), so the -19.5% is a house policy haircut, which the summary states once but §4 then contradicts with 'the price is already at our base-case value' (base is Rp1,635) and 'the equity is not worth the premium the market pays'.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck is read correctly (USD/IDR 18,350 FY2027E vs 17,968 spot, CPI 3.28, real GDP 5.29, terminal g 4.5% under the 5.0% cap, no royalty/concession parameters). But DVLA's COE of 10.51% is the lowest in its own PHARMA set — KLBF 12.04%, SIDO 12.02%, TSPC 12.37%, SOHO 11.02% — on the template default beta 0.70 (fund record beta_source 'industry default (config)'), not a DVLA or peer regression, and the report never reconciles the gap.

conservatism_audit.note: Stack of downward departures, each individually arguable: other non-operating income zeroed (+Rp9.4bn FY2025, +Rp14.6bn 9M-2026); GM floored at the trough with 1pt of recovery in five years; terminal reinvestment 47% of NOPAT (implied ROIC 9.6% versus 10.5% WACC, i.e. value destruction in perpetuity); no value for the medical-device entry beyond its capex. Scenarios are properly mirrored (revenue growth ±4pp, GM ±1.5pp, 50/25/25), so the asymmetry charge does not apply.

calibration.note: The D&A restatement is verified correct: note 9 shows 68,034,114 (FY2025) and 60,267,583 (FY2024), allocated 34.7 to cost of revenue, 20.3 to selling and 13.1 to administration, so Rp68.0bn/3.05% of revenue is the right charge. QC runs clean with no blocking flags and the -1.72pp FY2026E EBITDA-margin drift is the 9M LK arithmetic. Caveat: the Rp273.9bn 'FY2025 EBITDA' is the model's pre-other-income figure, not the LK's Rp284.3bn (see C10).

signoff.notes: Approved as initiated: SELL, target Rp940, price Rp1,570, TR -35.4%. The -35% call is honestly built: fundamental value Rp1,342 is about a seventh below the price (HOLD/REDUCE territory) and the 30% haircut is the house liquidity rule for ADTV below Rp100m (Rp55.7m over three months), disclosed on its own line in the summary and s4 rather than buried in WACC. Base case is now the reported nine months (group GM 49.9% vs 9M 49.93%, segment rebuild from note 28) and the margin path recovers to 51.6% by FY2030E, so the trough is not capitalised in perpetuity; scenarios are mirrored (+/-4pp growth, +/-1.5pp GM, 50/25/25) and the report states the rating comes from the haircut, not from an operating asymmetry. Record-level items for the next update, none of which moves the call: the model history still shows FY2025A dps 64 / payout 43.7% because the Rp41 interim is missing, so the pack contradicts the text's 'about three-quarters without a cut' and prints a 4.8% yield instead of about 6.7% (QC Q2, judge FIX); s4 renders shares as 'IDR1,120.0bn million' (QC Q1); the implied exit EV/EBITDA (3.56x) and terminal ROIIC should be printed rather than asserted (QC Q3).

bias.note: Base case is anchored on actuals: FY2026E revenue Rp2,521.9bn = reported 9M Rp1,848.5bn [S6] plus a Q4 at +11.5% yoy; gross margin held at the earned 9M level 49.9% (consumer 55.74%, prescription 42.07% [S6 p.82]) and recovers only half the prescription reset by FY2030; opex 44.4% = 9M actual plus a Q4 at the FY2025 Q4 intensity (54.8%) [S7]. Scenarios mirrored (+/-4pp growth, +/-1.5pp GM), base 50%. The engine calibration gap of -3.72pp is the documented 9M-2026 margin step, not an unsourced haircut. No default discount-war, strip-ratio or margin-squeeze assumption found. Residual conservatism is the 3.56x terminal exit multiple (finding Q3), which is not rating-changing.

findings.finding: Section 4 renders the share count as 'IDR1,120.0bn million' - the money filter is applied to the shares line - so the sentence carrying the float-placement arithmetic (80m shares) reads as nonsense.

Model history dps FY2025A = 64.00 (payout 43.7%) counts only the FY2025 final (Rp64/share, paid 2026, Rp71.68bn in the 9M-2026 cash-flow) and omits the FY2025 interim of Rp41/share / Rp45.9bn [S4]. Declared FY2025 DPS is about Rp105, payout about 72%, so the report's 'about three-quarters, without a cut' claim is right and the engine history is wrong. This is also the basis of the judge FIX.

Section 4 says the implied exit is 'below the multiple the stock trades on today' but never quantifies it.
